newsitem.title: POLAND: Ukraine's Kuchma in Poland to keep ties sweet.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma in Poland to keep ties sweet.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma began a visit to Warsaw on Thursday to cultivate a relationship both countries see as crucial to their interests and to be heaped with praise by Polish businesses for promoting trade.

Apart from collecting a man of the year award from the Polish Business Club employers' group for market reforms that have boosted bilateral trade, Kuchma was also meeting his counterpart Aleksander Kwasniewski and other Polish leaders.
"This is supposed to accent the very close, very friendly ties between Poland and Ukraine," Poland's Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told reporters before the one-day working visit.

Poland, well on the way to membership of the European Union and NATO, has enthusiastically adopted the role of advocate for its large but poorer ex-Soviet neighbour's efforts to bind itself closer to Central and Western European groupings.
This policy, partly designed to avoid the drawing of a new divide across Europe, is supported by Western states.

Ukraine, which regards Poland as a strategic partner, in turn raises no objections to Poland's key aim of joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- a goal strongly opposed by their common neighbour Russia.
Polish leaders have called for NATO to conclude a special charter or understanding with Ukraine, like that which the Western defence alliance is discussing with Russia.

Rosati said the two presidents were expected to oversee the signing of a memorandum, like one Poland clinched with Russia last year, on their desire to liberalise trade and create a mutual free trade zone in the future.

Poland's bilateral trade with Ukraine exceeded $1 billion for the first time in 1995 and from January to September last year totalled $1.4 billion -- a rise of 39 percent over the same period 1995, according to Polish economy ministry figures.

The data, quoted by PAP news agency, showed the balance of trade firmly in Poland's favour, with exports totalling $1 billion in the first nine months of 1996 and consisting of chemicals, coal, food products and electronics.
Poland, which imports mainly iron ore, chemicals and grain from Ukraine, also has investments in some 400 firms there.

Poland's political cooperation with Ukraine was underlined last year when the two presidents and Algirdas Brazauskas of Lithuania jointly voiced concern for democracy in Belarus, as President Alexander Lukashenko clashed with parliament.
Kwasniewski's spokesman said the two presidents would discuss Belarus plans for integration with Russia.
Despite the current official warmth, Poles and Ukrainians have sometimes been bitter foes.

Warsaw and Kiev have been drafting a declaration of reconciliation on painful past issues -- including a bloody revolt by Ukrainians in east Poland after World War Two which Warsaw's then-communist authorities ended by mass deportation.

Teams led by both presidents were to discuss this document on Thursday and Rosati said he hoped it could be signed this year. Polish officials believe it could be clinched during a visit by Kwasniewski to Ukraine, expected in May.
